title: What Travel Insurance Actually Covers in Thailand
content:
Travel insurance policies are sold as a single product and are really four or five separate coverages bundled together. The categories have specific meanings, and the gap between what a policy says it covers and what a traveller assumes it covers usually sits in the definitions rather than in the fine print. Here is what each category actually means.

Emergency medical

This covers sudden, unexpected illness or injury during the trip — treatment, hospital stays, doctor visits. It does not cover routine or planned care, and it does not cover follow-up treatment once you are home.

The word doing the work is "emergency." Something that develops gradually, or that you could reasonably have dealt with before departure, sits outside the category by design.

Evacuation and repatriation are two different things

These get conflated constantly, and a policy can include one without the other.

Medical evacuation moves a patient to the nearest facility capable of treating them. From a small Thai island, that generally means getting to Koh Samui, Phuket or Bangkok.

Repatriation returns a patient to their home country. That is a separate benefit, a separate cost, and a separate line in the policy schedule.

A policy with evacuation but no repatriation will get someone from Koh Tao to a Bangkok hospital and stop there.

Cancellation and interruption

Cancellation applies before departure — you paid for something and the trip did not happen. Interruption applies once the trip has started.

Interruption is the category that speaks to problems encountered abroad: a missed connection, a curtailed trip, unused prepaid nights. It is also the one people discover they do not have, because cancellation is the coverage that gets advertised.

The mechanic that matters most

Private Thai hospitals commonly require payment, or a guarantee of payment, before treating a foreign patient. What follows from that is the single most practically important thing in this article.

Direct billing means the hospital bills the insurer and the patient pays only a deductible. It happens when the insurer issues a guarantee of payment to that specific hospital — a document, arranged through the insurer's assistance line, not something the hospital produces on request.

Reimbursement means the patient pays the hospital and claims the money back afterwards.

The difference is not administrative. Under reimbursement, someone needs funds available at the moment of the emergency — potentially a large sum, on a card, in a country far from home. Under direct billing they do not. Which one applies depends on the insurer, the hospital and whether the assistance line was contacted before treatment rather than after.

How a claim actually runs

The sequence is consistent across policies:

  • Contact the insurer's assistance line as early as possible — ideally before treatment, because that is when a guarantee of payment can still be arranged.
  • Get treated. Thai hospitals issue itemised receipts, a doctor's report and proof of payment as standard.
  • Submit the documentation, if the treatment was not direct-billed.

The step that changes the outcome is the first one. Calling after treatment turns a potential direct-billing case into a reimbursement case.

Exclusion categories

Standard exclusions across the industry fall into a few groups: pre-existing conditions without a waiver, adventure activities without a rider, incidents involving alcohol or illegal acts, and routine or non-emergency care.

Adventure activities

Motorbike riding, scuba diving, zip-lining and rock climbing are commonly excluded or require a rider. The motorbike exclusion has a further condition attached — a valid motorcycle licence — which our guide to renting a scooter in Thailand covers in detail.

Pre-existing conditions

Commonly excluded unless a waiver is purchased, and waivers typically require the condition to have been stable for a defined period beforehand. That period varies by policy and is not something to assume.

What to compare

Because these are separate coverages, two policies at the same price can differ substantially in what they include. The categories above are the ones worth reading individually in any travel insurance policy rather than trusting a summary — and the direct-billing question is worth asking the insurer directly, since it does not usually appear in the schedule.

Where this sits in the trip

Insurance is generally bought early, in one sitting, weeks before departure — and most of what determines whether it pays out is settled later: where you stay, whether you end up riding something, which island you are on when something happens. Those decisions get made separately, by which time the policy is already bought.

How the coverage decision connects to the itinerary decisions that follow it is worked through in the complete Thailand trip guide.

FAQ

What is the difference between evacuation and repatriation?

Evacuation moves a patient to the nearest facility able to treat them. Repatriation returns them to their home country. They are separate coverages and a policy may include one without the other.

Will a Thai hospital bill my insurer directly?

Sometimes. Direct billing requires the insurer to issue a guarantee of payment to that hospital, arranged through the assistance line. Otherwise private hospitals commonly require payment upfront and the traveller claims back afterwards.

When should I call my insurer?

As early as possible, ideally before treatment — that is when a guarantee of payment can still be arranged. Calling afterwards generally means paying first and claiming back.

Is trip cancellation the same as trip interruption?

No. Cancellation applies before departure; interruption applies once the trip has started. Interruption is the one that covers problems encountered while abroad.

Are scooter accidents covered?

Motorbike riding is commonly excluded or requires a rider, and where it is covered there is usually a valid-licence condition attached. This varies by policy and is worth confirming in writing.
excerpt: The categories have specific meanings — and direct billing versus reimbursement decides whether you need funds at the moment of an emergency.

title: Medical Care in Thailand: What Exists Where
content:
Thailand has a well-developed medical system, and what a visitor encounters depends heavily on where they are when they need it. Bangkok and a small island are different countries medically. Here is what exists, what it costs, and how payment works.

Public and private

Thailand runs both systems, and foreign visitors overwhelmingly use the private one.

Private hospitals cost more, generally have English-speaking staff, and have shorter waits. Several in Bangkok are set up specifically for international patients, with dedicated international departments.

Public hospitals cost considerably less, have longer waits, and English varies with the institution and the individual. They are not inferior medically — Thailand's public system handles the country's population — but they are not organised around foreign visitors.

What exists where

The tier of care available drops sharply outside the main centres, and this is the fact worth knowing before you need it.

Bangkok has multiple internationally accredited private hospitals with full specialist departments — the top tier of care in the region.

Phuket and Koh Samui have full private hospitals capable of handling serious cases.

Koh Phangan, Koh Tao, Koh Lanta and Koh Chang have clinics or basic facilities rather than full hospitals. They can handle ordinary problems — infections, minor injuries, stomach trouble — and they stabilise rather than treat anything serious.

That last distinction is the one that matters. A clinic on a small island is a first response, not a destination. Anything beyond its scope means a transfer, which our guide to medical evacuation from Thai islands covers.

How payment works

Private hospitals typically require payment, or a guarantee of payment from an insurer, before non-emergency treatment. This surprises Americans used to being treated first and billed later.

A guarantee of payment is a document the insurer issues to the specific hospital, arranged through the insurer's assistance line. Without one, the patient pays and claims back afterwards — which means having the funds available at the time. Our guide to what travel insurance actually covers goes through that mechanic in detail.

Pharmacies

Thai pharmacies operate with a wider scope than American ones. Many medications that require a prescription in the United States are available over the counter, and pharmacists routinely advise on minor complaints.

For a visitor this cuts two ways: minor problems that would need a doctor's appointment at home can often be handled at a pharmacy counter, and medications that are tightly controlled at home may be easier to obtain than expected. What a pharmacy can dispense varies, and anything requiring a diagnosis is still a doctor's job.

Continuing a prescription

Refilling a US prescription in Thailand generally requires a consultation with a local doctor, who issues a Thai prescription. Bringing the original prescription and keeping medication in its labelled packaging makes that process straightforward.

Emergency numbers

The nationwide medical emergency number is 1669.

The Tourist Police line, 1155, is English-speaking and is frequently the more practical first call for a visitor who does not speak Thai — they can translate and coordinate. For a genuine medical emergency, 1669 is the number; for anything where the language barrier is itself the obstacle, 1155 is worth knowing.

What this connects to

Where you are staying determines what medical tier you are near, what an emergency transfer would involve, and how much a policy's evacuation coverage matters. Those are three separate things that get decided at three separate times — accommodation weeks out, insurance in a single sitting, and the emergency, if it comes, without warning.

How the medical picture connects to the base and island decisions is worked through in the complete Thailand trip guide.

FAQ

What is the emergency number in Thailand?

1669 for medical emergencies nationwide. The Tourist Police line, 1155, is English-speaking and is often the more practical first call for a visitor facing a language barrier.

Do Thai hospitals treat you before payment?

Private hospitals typically require payment or a guarantee of payment from an insurer before non-emergency treatment. A guarantee is arranged through the insurer's assistance line, not by the hospital.

Is there a hospital on Koh Tao?

Koh Tao has clinics rather than a full hospital. Koh Samui and Phuket have full private hospitals; Koh Phangan, Koh Lanta and Koh Chang have clinic-level facilities.

Can I buy medication over the counter in Thailand?

Thai pharmacies dispense many medications that require a prescription in the United States, and pharmacists advise on minor complaints. Anything requiring a diagnosis still needs a doctor.

Can I refill a US prescription in Thailand?

Generally through a consultation with a local doctor who issues a Thai prescription. Bringing the original prescription and keeping medication in labelled packaging helps.
excerpt: Bangkok and a small island are different countries medically. What each tier offers, and how payment works.

title: Medical Evacuation From Thai Islands
content:
The small Thai islands have clinics, not hospitals. Anything a clinic cannot handle means a transfer to Koh Samui, Phuket or Bangkok — and the mechanics of that transfer, who arranges it and what it costs, are almost never discussed before people travel. Here is how it works.

What is actually on each island

Koh Samui and Phuket have full private hospitals capable of handling serious cases without a transfer off the island.

Koh Phangan, Koh Tao, Koh Lanta and Koh Chang have clinics or basic facilities. They handle ordinary problems and stabilise serious ones. They do not treat them.

That difference is structural, not a matter of degree. On Samui a serious injury is treated where it happens. On Koh Tao it is stabilised and moved.

Hyperbaric chambers

Koh Tao has hyperbaric chamber facilities, which is worth stating explicitly because Koh Tao is one of the world's busiest dive-training destinations and decompression illness is the specific emergency the island generates most. Koh Phangan and Phuket also have chambers.

This is the one category where a small island has specialist capability that a larger one may not — the facilities follow the diving, not the population.

How a transfer physically happens

Two routes exist, and which applies depends on the island and the case.

Boat and ambulance is the ordinary path. A patient goes by boat to the mainland or to a larger island, then by road ambulance to a hospital. This is what happens for cases that are serious but stable.

Air ambulance is used where the island has an airstrip and the case warrants it — Koh Samui, Phuket and Krabi have airports. Koh Tao, Koh Phangan, Koh Lanta and Koh Chang do not, so an air evacuation from those islands is not a direct option.

Read those two lists together and the geography does something specific: the islands with clinic-level care rather than hospitals are largely the same islands with no airstrip. The place where a transfer is most likely to be needed is the place where it is slowest to arrange.

Who arranges it

The insurer's assistance line coordinates a medical evacuation with local providers. Not the patient, not usually the treating clinic, and not a family member calling from home.

The practical consequence is that the number that matters in a serious emergency abroad is the one printed on the insurance policy — and it is worth having it somewhere other than an email inbox on a phone that may be in a bag on a boat.

What it costs

Medical evacuation from a Thai island runs into the tens of thousands of US dollars, with a dedicated air ambulance at the higher end and a commercial flight with a medical escort at the lower.

This is the line item travel insurance exists for. It is also the coverage most commonly assumed rather than checked — and, as our guide to what travel insurance actually covers sets out, evacuation and repatriation are separate benefits, so a policy may fund the move to Bangkok without funding the flight home.

US domestic health insurance generally provides little or no coverage abroad and almost never covers evacuation.

What is not documented

Transfer timing is the honest gap. How long an island-to-Bangkok medical transfer typically takes is not reliably published, and it would depend on the island, the hour, the sea state and whether an air ambulance is available. Anyone quoting a confident figure is estimating.

How this connects to the island choice

Every element above is fixed before departure. Which islands have hospitals and which have clinics, which have airstrips and which do not, which have hyperbaric chambers — all of it is knowable when the itinerary is being built, and none of it is knowable in the moment it becomes relevant.

How the medical geography sits alongside the other reasons people pick islands is worked through in the complete Thailand trip guide.

FAQ

Which Thai islands have hospitals?

Koh Samui and Phuket have full private hospitals. Koh Phangan, Koh Tao, Koh Lanta and Koh Chang have clinics or basic facilities that stabilise serious cases rather than treating them.

Is there a hyperbaric chamber on Koh Tao?

Yes — Koh Tao has hyperbaric chamber facilities, which reflects its status as a major dive-training destination. Koh Phangan and Phuket also have chambers.

How does a medical evacuation from a Thai island work?

Either by boat then road ambulance, or by air ambulance where the island has an airstrip. Koh Samui, Phuket and Krabi have airports; Koh Tao, Koh Phangan, Koh Lanta and Koh Chang do not.

Who arranges a medical evacuation?

The insurer's assistance line coordinates it with local providers — not the patient and not usually the treating clinic. The number on the policy is the one that matters.

How much does medical evacuation cost in Thailand?

Into the tens of thousands of US dollars, with dedicated air ambulance at the higher end. US domestic health insurance generally does not cover it.
excerpt: Which islands have hospitals, which have airstrips, who arranges a transfer and what it costs.

title: How a Thai Visa Extension Actually Works
content:
Americans arriving in Thailand for tourism receive a visa exemption stamp at immigration. That stamp can usually be extended once, at an immigration office, for a fee. The process is routine and the details are rarely written down anywhere useful. Here they are.

What an extension gives you

A tourist extension adds 30 days to the permission already stamped in your passport. The fee is 1,900 baht, paid in cash at the immigration office.

It extends the existing permission rather than resetting it — the new date runs from the expiry of the current stamp, not from the date you apply.

Where to apply

At a Thai Immigration Bureau office. These exist in Bangkok and in the provincial centres, including the main tourist areas, so applying does not usually mean travelling far.

What to bring

  • Your passport
  • The TM7 application form (available at the office)
  • A passport-size photograph
  • Photocopies of your passport photo page and current entry stamp

Proof of your address in Thailand may also be requested. Requirements can vary between offices, and bringing more copies than you think you need costs nothing.

Timing

Processing is usually same-day, particularly if the application goes in early in the day. Some offices process while you wait; others take the passport for a few hours.

The application is made near the expiry of the current permission rather than well in advance. That timing has a consequence worth noticing: the extension has to happen while you are still legally in the country, in a particular place, during office hours, on a working day — which means it is a constraint on where you are in the last few days of your permitted stay, not just a piece of paperwork.

How many times

Commonly once per entry for a visa exemption or tourist visa. Anything beyond a single extension is discretionary rather than routine.

This is an area where policy has changed more than once, so the position at the time of a specific trip is worth confirming rather than assuming from any guide, including this one.

Border runs

Leaving Thailand and re-entering produces a new entry stamp. It is a different mechanism from an extension — a new permission rather than a longer one.

Repeated back-to-back entries attract additional scrutiny at immigration, and admission on a visa exemption is at the officer's discretion rather than automatic. Thai visa policy has tightened repeatedly in recent years, and the practical reception of frequent border runs has moved with it.

Check the stamp

The date written on the entry stamp is the date that governs — not the length of the exemption in the abstract, and not what a booking site said. Immigration officers write an "admitted until" date, and that is the legal deadline.

Verifying it before leaving the immigration desk takes a few seconds. What happens when the assumed date and the stamped date differ is covered in our guide to entry refusal and overstay in Thailand.

Where this sits in a trip

Whether an extension is needed at all depends on trip length, and whether it is convenient depends on where the itinerary has you in its final week. Those get decided months apart — trip length when flights are booked, position in the last week when the route is planned — and the extension question only surfaces at the intersection.

How the entry rules interact with itinerary length and shape is worked through in the complete Thailand trip guide.

FAQ

How long is a Thai tourist extension?

30 days, added to the permission already stamped in your passport. The new date runs from the expiry of the current stamp, not from the application date.

How much does a visa extension cost in Thailand?

1,900 baht, paid in cash at a Thai Immigration Bureau office.

What do I need for a Thai visa extension?

Passport, the TM7 form available at the office, a passport photo, and photocopies of your passport photo page and entry stamp. Proof of address may also be requested, and requirements vary between offices.

Can I extend more than once?

Commonly once per entry for a visa exemption or tourist visa. Beyond that is discretionary, and this is an area where policy has changed more than once.

Does a border run work instead?

Leaving and re-entering produces a new entry stamp rather than an extension. Repeated back-to-back entries attract additional scrutiny, and admission on a visa exemption is at the officer's discretion.
excerpt: Thirty days, 1,900 baht, and a checklist — the process the guides mention but never describe.

title: Thailand Overstay and Entry Rules: The Penalty Structure
content:
Thailand's overstay rules are written down, specific, and structured in a way that rewards one behaviour heavily over another. The fine is small and capped. The consequence that scales is the re-entry ban. Here is the structure.

The fine

Overstaying costs 500 baht per day, capped at 20,000 baht. The cap is reached at 40 days, and the fine stops accumulating after that.

It is paid at the immigration counter on departure, at an airport or a land border. Officers calculate the days, collect the fine and issue a receipt before stamping you out.

One thing worth knowing that rarely gets mentioned: for an overstay of a few hours caused by a flight delay or a schedule change, the fine is usually waived if you explain the situation to the immigration officer at departure. The Royal Thai Embassy states this directly. A missed connection that pushes you past midnight is not the scenario the penalty structure is aimed at.

The ban is what scales

The fine stops growing at 40 days. The re-entry ban does not, and this is the part that matters.

Where someone surrenders voluntarily — presenting at immigration on departure or at an office while still in the country:

  • Under 90 days: fine only, no ban
  • Over 90 days: up to a 1-year ban
  • Over 1 year: up to a 3-year ban
  • Over 3 years: up to a 5-year ban
  • Over 5 years: up to a 10-year ban

Being caught rather than surrendering carries substantially harsher consequences, including detention at an immigration facility before deportation, and a longer ban. The cash fine is identical either way.

So the structure prices the act rather than the wallet: a 41-day overstay and a five-year overstay cost the same money, and differ entirely in whether Thailand is available afterwards.

The date that governs

The "admitted until" date written on the entry stamp is the legal deadline. Not the exemption length in the abstract, not what an airline or booking site said, not a calculation from the arrival date.

Officers write that date by hand or stamp it, and it is worth reading before leaving the desk. Our guide to the visa extension process covers what to do if the stamped date is shorter than the trip.

Onward tickets — who actually checks

Proof of onward or return travel is a requirement, and the party that enforces it is usually the airline at check-in rather than Thai immigration on arrival.

That distinction is practical. An airline that will not board you leaves you at your departure airport, on your own time and money, with no Thai official involved. The requirement is most likely to bite thousands of miles before Thailand.

Proof of funds

A funds requirement exists in the regulations — commonly cited as 20,000 baht per person or 40,000 per family — and it is not routinely checked in practice. It remains a legal requirement that an officer may ask about, and the honest description is a rule that exists and is enforced inconsistently.

The arrival card

The Thailand Digital Arrival Card replaced the paper TM6 form in May 2025. It is mandatory for foreign nationals, free, and filed online before arrival at the official immigration site.

The filing window has changed since introduction, so the current timing is worth checking on the official site rather than taking from any guide. Our guide to visa requirements for Americans covers the arrival card in more detail.

Repeated entries

Back-to-back visa-exempt entries attract additional scrutiny, and admission on an exemption is at the officer's discretion rather than automatic. Thai policy in this area has tightened repeatedly, and what was routine in one year has not always been routine in the next.

How this connects to the rest

Every deadline here is set at the immigration desk on arrival, and every decision that interacts with it — trip length, where you are in the final week, whether an extension is practical — is made either months before or days before. They are never made at the same time, and the stamp is the only one of them written down.

How the entry deadlines interact with itinerary shape is worked through in the complete Thailand trip guide.

FAQ

What is the overstay fine in Thailand?

500 baht per day, capped at 20,000 baht. The cap is reached at 40 days and the fine stops accumulating after that. It is paid at immigration on departure.

What happens if I overstay by a few hours?

For a short overstay caused by a flight delay or schedule change, the fine is usually waived if explained to the immigration officer at departure — the Royal Thai Embassy states this directly.

Will overstaying get me banned from Thailand?

Under 90 days with a voluntary surrender is a fine with no ban. Over 90 days brings a ban of a year or more, scaling with duration. Being caught rather than surrendering carries harsher consequences including detention.

Do I need an onward ticket for Thailand?

It is a requirement, and it is usually enforced by the airline at check-in rather than by Thai immigration on arrival — so it tends to bite before you leave home.

Is proof of funds actually checked?

Not routinely, though it remains a legal requirement an officer may ask about. The commonly cited figures are 20,000 baht per person or 40,000 per family.
excerpt: The fine caps at 40 days. The re-entry ban does not — and that is the part that scales.
